# Delirium

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Neurology > Disorders of consciousness > Delirium*

[Original Article Link](/library/6P0jfT)

---

## Summary

Delirium is a neurocognitive disorder characterized by impairments in attention and awareness (reduced orientation to the environment), as well as other cognitive disturbances (e.g., in <u>memory</u>, language, or perception). Symptoms develop acutely and tend to fluctuate throughout the day. Delirium occurs most commonly in older patients and is typically secondary to another medical condition or <u>polypharmacy</u>. As delirium is common in critically ill patients, prevention is also part of <u>supportive care in the ICU</u>. Although delirium is a reversible confusional state, it warrants urgent medical attention because it may be the first sign of serious underlying disease. <u>Management of delirium</u> focuses on treating the underlying illness and providing <u>supportive care</u> until the confusion resolves. <u>Antipsychotic medications</u> may be used to <u>manage agitation</u> if other measures fail.




![Delirium](media/x41zk2297ktqsbl0vvqgefbv.jpg)

Delirium

---

## Etiology

Delirium is typically secondary to another medical condition or <u>polypharmacy</u>. The following is a nonexhaustive list of common causes of delirium.




### Metabolic diseases




* Most common cause; also referred to as metabolic encephalopathy

* Etiologies include:

* <u>Liver</u> or <u>kidney failure</u>

* <u>Diabetes mellitus</u> (<u>diabetic ketoacidosis</u>)

* <u>Hyperthyroidism</u> or <u>hypothyroidism</u>

* <u>Vitamin deficiencies</u> (e.g., <u>vitamin B<sub>12</sub> deficiency</u>, <u>folate deficiency</u>, <u>thiamine deficiency</u>)

* <u>Electrolyte</u> abnormalities





### Infection




* <u>UTIs</u> (most common cause in older patients)

* <u>Pneumonia</u>

* <u>Meningitis</u>





### <u>CNS</u> pathology




* <u>Ischemic stroke</u>

* <u>Intracranial hemorrhage</u>

* <u>Brain tumor</u>





### Drugs (<u>drug-induced cognitive impairment</u>) and toxins (toxic <u>encephalopathy</u>)




* <u>Anticholinergics</u>

* <u>Benzodiazepines</u>, <u>barbiturates</u>

* <u>Antidepressants</u> and <u>antipsychotics</u> (especially those with <u>anticholinergic</u> activity, e.g., <u>quetiapine</u>)

* <u>Antihistamines</u> (particularly in older patients)

* <u>Opioids</u>

* <u>Diuretics</u> (may cause <u>electrolyte</u> abnormalities)

* <u>Recreational drugs</u> (intoxication/withdrawal)

* <u>Alcohol use disorder</u> and <u>alcohol withdrawal</u>

* Heavy metals (e.g., <u>arsenic</u>, lead, <u>mercury</u>)





### Cardiorespiratory conditions




* <u>Hypoxia</u> (e.g., <u>anemia</u>, <u>pulmonary embolism</u>)

* <u>Hypercapnia</u> (e.g., <u>COPD</u>)

* Acute cardiovascular disease

* <u>Myocardial infarction</u>

* <u>Shock</u>

* <u>Acute heart failure</u>

* <u>Dehydration</u>





### Other




* <u>Constipation</u>

* <u>Urinary retention</u>

* Major <u>surgery</u>

* Trauma (e.g., <u>hip fracture</u>, <u>traumatic brain injury</u>)

* <u>Pain</u>

* <u>Sleep deprivation</u>

* <u>Hearing</u> or <u>vision loss</u>





> [!NOTE]
> Pediatric, older (> 65 years), and hospitalized patients are particularly susceptible to delirium. [[3]](/library/eJaxGl)[[4]](/library/LgYwDo)[[5]](/library/e7Yxkq)




> [!NOTE]
> I WATCH DEATH: Infection, Withdrawal, Acute metabolic disorder, Trauma, CNS pathology, Hypoxia, Deficiencies, Endocrine, Acute vascular, Toxins/drugs, and Heavy metals are the major causes of delirium.

---

## Clinical features

* The main symptom is an acute (hours to days) alteration in the level of awareness and attention.

* Other features may include:

* <u>Disorganized thinking</u>

* <u>Illusions</u>

* <u>Hallucinations</u> (mostly visual)

* Cognitive deficits (e.g., <u>memory</u>)

* Reversal of the <u>sleep</u>-wake cycle

* Emotional lability

* <u>Agitation</u>, combativeness

* Alterations in psychomotor activity may occur.

* The severity of symptoms fluctuates throughout the day and worsens in the evening (termed <u>sundowning</u>).

* Symptoms are reversible; their duration and severity depend on the underlying illness.

* Delirium is commonly described based on the type of alteration that is seen:





|  | Psychomotor activity | Patient groups |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mixed type delirium | Fluctuates or stays at baseline | Most common type in the general population |
| Hypoactive delirium | Decreased | Most common type in the older population |
| Hyperactive delirium | Increased (<u>agitation</u>) | Usually seen in delirium due to substance use or <u>substance withdrawal</u><br> |

---

## Diagnosis

Delirium is <u>diagnosed clinically</u>, based on either the <u>DSM 5</u> or Confusion Assessment Method (<u>CAM</u>) criteria. Further studies should be conducted to determine the underlying etiology.




> [!WARNING]
> Delirium should be considered a <u>medical emergency</u> until proven otherwise; it can be a sign of severe underlying pathology and is associated with increased mortality. [[5]](/library/e7Yxkq)




### Diagnostic criteria [[6]](/library/Nta-dm)[[7]](/library/xdXEHC)




#### <u>Confusion assessment method</u> (<u>CAM</u>) [[8]](/library/9dXNHC)




<u>CAM</u> can be used in the community and most hospital environments to assess delirium; for patients in the <u>ICU</u> or the recovery room, use the modified version, <u>CAM-ICU</u>. [[9]](/library/lrYvhq)




| <br>Confusion assessment method (<u>CAM</u>) [[7]](/library/xdXEHC)[[8]](/library/9dXNHC)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Feature | Definition | Description |
| Feature 1 | <br>* Acute onset with fluctuating course<br><br> | <br>* The patient has the following: <br><br>* <u>Change in mental status</u> from baseline<br><br>* Fluctuating <u>level of consciousness</u>, attention, speech, and/or disordered thinking<br><br> |
| Feature 2 | <br>* Inattention<br><br> | <br>* The patient has trouble focusing, keeping track of the conversation, or can be easily distracted.<br><br> |
| Feature 3 | <br>* Thinking is disorganized.<br><br> | <br>* The patient's speech is unclear, they seem incoherent, or the flow of ideas is illogical.<br><br> |
| Feature 4 | <br>* Altered consciousness<br><br> | <br>* The patient may be either:<br><br>* <u>Hypervigilant</u><br><br>* Drowsy, <u>lethargic</u>, stuporous, or <u>comatose</u><br><br> |
| Diagnosis of delirium requires features 1 and 2 PLUS either feature 3 or 4. |  |  |





#### DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for delirium [[6]](/library/Nta-dm)




The patient meets all of the following:




* Attention and awareness are impaired.

* Acute onset over hours or days with waxing and waning severity

* ≥ 1 additional disruption in <u>cognition</u>

* The condition fulfills the following criteria:

* Absence of preexisting <u>dementia</u>, <u>coma</u>, or severely reduced responsiveness

* Evidence of an organic underlying cause





### Determination of the underlying etiology




#### Routine <u>laboratory studies</u> [[7]](/library/xdXEHC)[[10]](/library/mQXV9B)




The following studies are recommended in all patients with a new presumptive delirium diagnosis.




* <u>Complete blood count</u>

* Serum <u>glucose</u>

* <u>Electrolytes</u>

* <u>Urinalysis</u>: abnormalities related to <u>UTI</u> (e.g., <u>pyuria</u>, <u>bacteriuria</u>) or <u>renal failure</u> (e.g., <u>urinary casts</u>)

* <u>Urea</u> and <u>creatinine</u>

* <u>Magnesium</u>

* <u>Liver chemistries</u>





#### Further diagnostic studies




These should be guided by clinical suspicion of the underlying process or conducted if no other cause has been identified with routine tests.




| Symptom-based diagnostic workup for delirium |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Suspected underlying process | Concerning features | Diagnostic studies |
| Intracranial | <br><br>* History of trauma, especially in patients on anticoagulation<br><br>* <u>Focal neurological symptoms</u><br><br>* <u>Seizure</u>  [[11]](/library/wdXhHC)<br><br>* <u>Fever</u> with <u>headache</u> or <u>meningismus</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Neuroimaging</u> (CT head or <u>MRI</u> head)<br><br>* <u>EEG</u>: usually shows diffuse slowing of background activity in patients with delirium  [[11]](/library/wdXhHC)<br><br>* <u>Lumbar puncture</u> and <u>CSF analysis</u><br><br><br> |
| Pulmonary | <br><br>* <u>Fever</u> with <u>cough</u> or <u>shortness of breath</u><br><br>* <u>Risk factors for aspiration pneumonia</u><br><br>* Conditions associated with<br><br>* <u>Hypoxemic respiratory failure</u>, e.g., <u>pulmonary embolism</u> (<u>PE</u>)<br><br>* <u>Hypercapnic respiratory failure</u>, e.g., <u>CO<sub>2</sub> narcosis</u> in <u>COPD</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Chest <u>x-ray</u><br><br>* <u>Arterial blood gas</u><br><br>* <u>CTPA</u><br><br><br> |
| Cardiac | <br><br>* Abnormal <u>hemodynamics</u><br><br>* <u>Chest pain</u><br><br>* Worsening <u>peripheral edema</u> and/or <u>shortness of breath</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>ECG</u><br><br>* <u>Echocardiogram</u><br><br><br> |
| Nutritional (e.g., <u>vitamin deficiencies</u>) | <br><br>* History of <u>heavy drinking</u><br><br>* <u>Malabsorption</u><br><br>* <u>Malnutrition</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Vitamin B<sub>12</sub></u>, <u>folate</u>, and <u>thiamine</u> levels<br><br> |
| Toxic (e.g., intoxication or withdrawal) | <br><br>* History of <u>alcohol</u> or <u>recreational drug</u> use<br><br>* Suspicion of <u>CO poisoning</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Consider urine toxicology or serum drug levels  [[12]](/library/-oXDe_)<br><br>* <u>CIWA</u> score (see also “<u>Delirium tremens</u>”)<br><br>* <u>Carboxyhemoglobin</u> levels<br><br><br> |
| Infectious | <br><br>* <u>Fever</u><br><br>* <u>qSOFA score</u> ≥ 2<br><br>* <u>Risk factors for bloodborne diseases</u> or <u>STIs</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Bacterial cultures (e.g., urine, or <u>blood culture</u>)<br><br>* Serum <u>lactate</u><br><br>* <u>HIV</u>, <u>syphilis serology</u><br><br><br> |
| Endocrine | <br><br>* <u>Clinical features of thyrotoxicosis</u> or of <u>thyroid storm</u><br><br>* <u>Clinical features of hypothyroidism</u>, including <u>myxedema coma</u><br><br>* Features of <u>adrenal crisis</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Thyroid function tests</u><br><br>* <u>Cortisol</u> level<br><br><br> |
| Hepatic | <br><br>* History of <u>hepatitis</u> or <u>alcohol</u> use<br><br>* Use of <u>hepatotoxic</u> medications<br><br>* <u>Clinical features of liver failure</u><br><br>* <u>Stigmata of chronic liver disease</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Liver</u> <u>ultrasound</u><br><br>* Serum <u>ammonia</u>  [[13]](/library/AoXRe_)<br><br><br> |
| Renal | <br><br>* <u>Uremia</u><br><br>* <u>Anuria</u> or <u>oliguria</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Ultrasound</u> abdomen/<u>pelvis</u> (<u>urinary tract</u>)<br><br> |
| <br>Psychiatric  [[14]](/library/BoXzV_)<br> | <br><br>* <u>Risk factors</u> for <u>major depressive disorder</u><br><br>* <u>Depressive disorder</u> may manifest as<br><br>* <u>Major depressive disorder with atypical features</u><br><br>* <u>Major depressive disorder with psychotic features</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Depression screening</u><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> Diagnosis of delirium is clinical. Identify the underlying precipitating factors for DELIRIUM: Drugs, Electrolyte abnormalities, Lack of medication (withdrawal), Infection, Reduced sensorial input, Intracranial pathology, Urinary retention or <u>fecal impaction</u>, Myocardial and pulmonary disease. [[7]](/library/xdXEHC)

---

## Differential diagnoses

The symptoms of delirium overlap with a number of other neurological disorders, including <u>dementia</u>. Additionally, patients with preexisting neurological diseases such as <u>dementia</u> are more vulnerable to developing delirium.




### <u>Dementia</u>




Delirium is most often confused with <u>dementia</u>. However, there are significant differences in the presentation of diseases.




| <br>Delirium vs. dementia [[15]](/library/4N13Yh0) |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Delirium | <u>Dementia</u> |
| Onset | <br><br>* Sudden<br><br>* <u>Prodromal</u> phase might precede<br><br><br> | <br>* Insidious<br><br> |
| Course | <br><br>* Rapid and fluctuating<br><br>* Hours to days<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Slowly progressive deterioration<br><br>* Months to years<br><br><br> |
| <u>Level of consciousness</u> | <br>* Impaired (fluctuating)<br><br> | <br>* Usually alert<br><br> |
| Attention | <br>* Impaired (fluctuating)<br><br> | <br><br>* Usually intact<br><br>* Impaired in the advanced phase<br><br><br> |
| <u>Memory</u> | <br>* Recent <u>memory</u> loss<br><br> | <br>* Recent, then remote <u>memory</u> loss<br><br> |
| <u>Thought process</u> | <br>* Disorganized<br><br> | <br>* Impoverished<br><br> |
| <u>Hallucinations</u> | <br>* Present (often visual or tactile)<br><br> | <br>* Can be present in advanced disease<br><br> |
| Psychomotor activity | <br>* Increased or decreased<br><br> | <br>* Usually normal<br><br> |
| <u>EEG</u> | <br>* Usually abnormal<br><br> | <br>* Usually normal<br><br> |
| Reversibility | <br>* Reversible<br><br> | <br>* Usually irreversible<br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> Delirium is characterized by acute onset of fluctuations in attention and <u>level of consciousness</u>. In <u>dementia</u>, the onset is insidious and attention and <u>level of consciousness</u> are typically preserved until the advanced phase. [[15]](/library/4N13Yh0)




### Other [[16]](/library/DdX1HC)




* <u>Hydrocephalus</u> (e.g., <u>normal pressure hydrocephalus</u>)

* <u>Osmotic demyelination syndrome</u>

* <u>Hypertensive encephalopathy</u>

* <u>Herpes encephalitis</u>

* <u>Chronic subdural hematoma</u>

* Other <u>causes of altered mental status</u>





The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Management

### General principles




For the approach to undifferentiated patients with <u>altered mental status</u>, see “<u>Initial management of AMS</u>.”




* Treatment of the underlying condition: the mainstay of management

* Consider discontinuing;  or reducing the dose of causative medications, e.g., <u>anticholinergics</u>.  [[7]](/library/xdXEHC)[[10]](/library/mQXV9B)

* See “Etiology” for a detailed list of conditions.

* <u>Supportive care</u>: Clinical manifestations, functional limitations, and associated risks of delirium can persist, requiring admission and <u>supportive care</u>.

* Behavioral emergencies: See “<u>Treatment of agitation in delirium</u>.”





> [!WARNING]
> Do not discharge patients from ambulatory settings unless delirium resolves with initial management and an underlying cause has been identified and treated. [[17]](/library/35YSPp)




> [!TIP]
> In patients requiring admission, consider a higher <u>level of care</u> based on clinical status and monitoring needs.




### <u>Supportive care</u> [[7]](/library/xdXEHC)[[10]](/library/mQXV9B)[[16]](/library/DdX1HC)




* Patient comfort and symptom control

* <u>Fever</u> control and <u>pain management</u> (preferably with nonopioid medications)  [[10]](/library/mQXV9B)

* Maintain adequate hydration and nutrition (see “<u>IV fluid therapy</u>”).

* Evaluate and treat <u>urinary retention</u> or <u>fecal impaction</u> if present.

* Mobilize the patient as soon as possible.

* Reducing confusion

* Reorient the patient to time, place, and person  [[7]](/library/xdXEHC)

* Initiate <u>cognitive stimulation therapy</u> to improve cognitive function.

* See also “Prevention.”

* Prevention of complications [[7]](/library/xdXEHC)

* <u>Prevention of decubitus ulcers</u> (e.g., mobilization, toilet program)

* <u>Aspiration precautions</u>

* Fall prevention

* Minimize the use of <u>physical restraints</u>.





> [!TIP]
> A comprehensive care strategy involving multidisciplinary health providers and family members is preferred to prevent and address complications of delirium. [[7]](/library/xdXEHC)

---

## Treatment of agitation in delirium

Patients with delirium may become <u>agitated</u> or aggressive as a result of acute confusion, particularly in unfamiliar environments.




* For <u>agitation</u> in patients with <u>dementia</u>, see “<u>Management of dementia</u>.”

* For more comprehensive management, see also “<u>Management of the agitated patient</u>.”





### Nonpharmacological measures




<u>Agitation</u> should initially be managed with nonpharmacologic strategies.




* Continue <u>supportive care</u> (e.g., reassurance, reorientation).

* Arrange for a family member or sitter to remain with the patient at all times.

* Identify and treat easily reversible <u>causes of agitation</u>: e.g., <u>dehydration</u>, hunger, <u>pain</u>, <u>hypoxia</u>, or <u>urinary retention</u>.

* Use <u>de-escalation techniques</u>: e.g., calm verbal interaction, clear communication. [[18]](/library/2QXTvB)





> [!WARNING]
> Avoid <u>physical restraints</u> as much as possible in older patients with delirium, as they can worsen <u>distress</u> and <u>agitation</u>, as well as contribute to preventable injuries. [[19]](/library/kKXmg_)




### Pharmacotherapy [[7]](/library/xdXEHC)




Medications should be reserved for refractory <u>agitation</u>.




* Sedating medications should be limited to patients with <u>agitation</u> severe enough to pose a risk to themselves or others.

* To minimize the risk of worsening delirium with medication:

* Check for <u>drug interactions</u>.

* Start with the lowest possible dose.

* Titrate until <u>agitation</u> reduces.

* Discontinue the drug as soon as possible.

* Consider specialist consultation (e.g., <u>psychiatry</u>, geriatrics) for patients who need continual dosing.

* The recommended dosages for older adults are lower than for younger patients.  [[7]](/library/xdXEHC)[[20]](/library/_oX5e_)





#### <u>Antipsychotics</u> [[7]](/library/xdXEHC)[[20]](/library/_oX5e_)




* Agents

* <u>Typical antipsychotics</u>: e.g., <u>haloperidol</u>  DOSAGE (most commonly used)  [[20]](/library/_oX5e_)

* <u>Atypical antipsychotic</u> options   [[20]](/library/_oX5e_); 

* <u>Risperidone</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Olanzapine</u> DOSAGE

* Adverse effects  

* Sedation

* Increased risk of falls

* <u>Extrapyramidal symptoms</u>

* Lowered <u>seizure</u> threshold





> [!WARNING]
> Avoid <u>antipsychotics</u> in patients with underlying <u>alcohol withdrawal</u> or <u>benzodiazepine withdrawal</u> (due to the risk of <u>seizures</u>) and in patients at high risk for <u>QTc prolongation</u> (due to the risk of <u>torsades de pointes</u>). [[9]](/library/lrYvhq)




#### <u>Benzodiazepines</u> [[7]](/library/xdXEHC)[[10]](/library/mQXV9B)[[20]](/library/_oX5e_)




* Clinical applications: Reserve for patients with <u>alcohol</u> or <u>benzodiazepine withdrawal</u>, or a history of <u>neuroleptic malignant syndrome</u>. [[10]](/library/mQXV9B)

* Preferred agent: <u>lorazepam</u> DOSAGE

* Adverse effects

* Prolonged or worsening delirium

* <u>Oversedation</u> and falls





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Benzodiazepines</u> are deliriogenic. Do not treat delirious patients with <u>benzodiazepines</u> unless the delirium is due to <u>alcohol</u> or <u>benzodiazepine withdrawal</u>.

---

## Prevention

> [!TIP]
> Over one-third of cases of delirium can be prevented with nonpharmacological strategies. [[5]](/library/e7Yxkq)




* The following measures can reduce <u>morbidity</u>: [[21]](/library/KdXUIC)

* Early identification of at-risk patients (see “Etiology”)

* Regular screening to detect early signs of delirium

* Tailored care according to risk, e.g., validated monitoring tools and prevention strategies for older patients [[9]](/library/lrYvhq)[[10]](/library/mQXV9B)[[21]](/library/KdXUIC)

* Delirium is very common in the <u>ICU</u>; see “<u>Supportive care in the ICU</u>” for additional considerations. [[22]](/library/IlXYyy)





> [!TIP]
> Older patients are at particularly high risk for delirium during hospitalization and benefit from specialized monitoring and prevention. [[21]](/library/KdXUIC)




### Prevention strategies




* Nonpharmacologic prophylaxis

* Reduce exposure to <u>modifiable risk factors</u>.

* Avoid drugs that can worsen delirium (e.g., <u>benzodiazepines</u>, <u>anticholinergics</u>, <u>opioids</u>).

* Avoid restraints if possible.

* Ensure that the patient is comfortable and that symptoms are well controlled (see “<u>Supportive care</u>” in “Management” section).

* Reorient the patient regularly.

* Keep a clock and/or calendar near the patient to help with orientation.

* Provide visual and <u>hearing aids</u> for patients with impairments.

* Keep curtains open and lights on during daytime hours.

* At night, reduce the amount of noise, procedures, and medication administration.

* <u>Disorientation</u> may be worse if the patient is awoken at night.

* Uninterrupted <u>sleep</u> is important for both prevention and <u>management of delirium</u>.

* See also “<u>Inpatient management of insomnia</u>.”

* Arrange for regular visits from family and friends.

* Regularly assess at-risk patients using the <u>CAM</u> tool to detect delirium early.

* Pharmacological prophylaxis: Some medications (e.g., <u>dexmedetomidine</u>, <u>melatonin</u>) have been used to prevent delirium in the critical care/postoperative settings, but benefits are still uncertain.  [[16]](/library/DdX1HC)





> [!TIP]
> Uninterrupted <u>sleep</u> is particularly important in patients with delirium, who may experience a worsening of neuropsychiatric symptoms in the evening and at night known as <u>sundowning</u>.




> [!WARNING]
> <u>Cholinesterase inhibitors</u> have not been shown to be effective in the prevention or <u>treatment of delirium</u>. However, patients requiring long-term treatment <u>cholinesterase inhibitors</u> can continue to use them. [[23]](/library/lQXvwB)[[24]](/library/8lXOAy)
